design_detail: Multicentre case-control study within the EU-GEI programme (work package 2). Cases: 901 people aged 18 to 64 presenting with a first episode of psychosis (ICD-10 F20-F33; research diagnosis by the OPCRIT algorithm) to mental health services in 11 catchment areas: London and Cambridge (UK), Amsterdam and Gouda and Voorhout (Netherlands), Paris Val-de-Marne and Puy de Dôme (France), Madrid and Barcelona (Spain), Bologna and Palermo (Italy) and Ribeirão Preto (Brazil). Controls: 1237 people from the same areas recruited by quota sampling and weighted to the population at risk. Recruitment 1 May 2010 to 1 April 2015. Exposure by interview (modified Cannabis Experience Questionnaire); potency assigned from the type of cannabis named, using European and national data on mean THC by type (high potency: THC 10% or more). Logistic regression with inverse-probability weights and site clustering; population attributable fractions computed assuming causality; and a site-level (ecological) correlation of cannabis-use prevalence in controls with incidence rates from the EU-GEI incidence study.
can_establish: Whether people with a first episode of psychosis reported daily use and use of high-potency types of cannabis more often than population controls from the same areas, after adjustment for demographics, education, employment, tobacco and other drug use, and how much that association varied between sites.
cannot_establish: That cannabis caused the psychotic disorders (familial and genetic liability, childhood adversity and other factors were not measured, and use during a prodrome is not excluded); how many cases removing high-potency cannabis would prevent (the attributable fractions assume the adjusted odds ratios are causal and that nothing replaces the removed exposure); or that site differences in cannabis use explain site differences in incidence (an ecological correlation across 10 sites).

sample.recruitment: Cases: everyone presenting with a first episode of psychosis to mental health services in each catchment area, identified by trained researchers through regular checks of the services and approached through their clinical team (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph). Controls: quota sampling to match each catchment's population at risk on age, gender and ethnicity, mostly by random sampling from lists of postal addresses and from general-practice lists of randomly selected surgeries, with internet and newspaper advertisements and leaflets used to oversample hard-to-reach groups such as young men; each control was weighted by the inverse of the probability of selection given age, gender and ethnicity, using census data (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cases: aged 18 to 64, resident in the catchment area at first presentation with an ICD-10 psychosis diagnosis (F20-F33); excluded if previously treated for psychosis, or if they met criteria for organic psychosis (F09) or psychotic symptoms from acute intoxication (F1X.5). Controls: excluded if they had ever been diagnosed with or treated for a psychotic disorder (Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Controls versus cases (Table 1): mean age 36.0 (SD 12.8) vs 31.2 (10.6) years; women 53.0% vs 38.1%; white 75.2% vs 59.0%, Black 9.5% vs 18.6%, mixed 9.1% vs 11.5%, North African 1.9% vs 4.7%; no school qualifications 5.3% vs 17.5%, postgraduate education 14.3% vs 4.0%; unemployed one year before assessment 7.7% vs 18.8%.
sample.attrition: Of 1519 cases approached, 356 (23%) refused, 19 (1%) could not consent because of language and 14 (0.9%) were outside the age range, leaving 1130 participants; refusers were older (p = 0.0015), more often women (p = 0.0063) and more often of white European origin (p < 0.0001) (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Maison Blanche recruited no controls and was excluded; Verona, Santiago, Oviedo, Valencia and Cuenca had at least 10% missing data on cannabis measures or main confounders and were excluded, leaving 901 of 1130 cases (80%) and 1237 of 1499 controls (83%) (editors' arithmetic) in a complete-case analysis (Results, 3rd paragraph). The number of controls approached and their response are not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: Participating cases were younger than the full incidence sample (mean 31.2 vs 34.5 years; Results, 2nd paragraph). If the older, female and white European patients who refused used cannabis less often, the participating cases over-represent cannabis use and the odds ratios are biased upward; this is not examined. Control participation is unknown, and advertising to reach under-represented groups could select controls whose drug use differs from that of the population. Excluding six of the 17 sites removes most of the Spanish and some of the Italian data.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in interview: the Medical Research Council Sociodemographic Schedule and an updated modified Cannabis Experience Questionnaire (CEQ EU-GEI); recruitment materials did not mention cannabis or its possible role; questions about the type of cannabis did not refer to potency and allowed the colloquial name in any language; no biological verification (Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 8th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Six measures: lifetime use (ever or never), current use, first use at age 15 or younger, lifetime frequency (the frequency of the person's most consistent pattern: never or occasional, more than once a week, daily), spending of at least €20 a week during that pattern, and potency. Potency was assigned from the type named, using the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction 2016 report and national data on mean THC by type: low (THC below 10%) or high (THC 10% or more); CBD was not included because reliable data existed only for England and the Netherlands (Methods › Measures, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph). The main text does not say whether the most consistent pattern had to precede the onset of psychosis; the questionnaire is in the appendix, not read (Gage's linked comment states that use before the first-episode diagnosis was asked about). Current use at assessment, unlike the lifetime pattern, was not associated after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9 to 1.5, p = 0.36; Table 2). Route was not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco (10 or more cigarettes a day vs fewer or none) and ever use of stimulants, hallucinogens, ketamine and novel psychoactive substances (legal highs) were included in the fully adjusted models. The Methods also name mean daily alcoholic drinks among the confounders, but the Table 2 footnote does not list alcohol, which did not differ between groups (p = 0.45) (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2 footnote).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (exposure history). Current use was recorded at assessment, after onset in the cases.

comparison.controls: Population controls without a psychotic disorder from the same catchment areas, recruited by quota sampling and weighted to the population at risk by age, gender and ethnicity.
comparison.matching: Frequency matching through quotas on age, gender and ethnicity, plus inverse-probability weights. The estimates labelled crude are adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity; the fully adjusted estimates add education, employment status, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs and hallucinogens (Table 2 footnote). Confounders were chosen by testing their association with case status (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of family history of psychosis, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid functioning or IQ, or of symptoms before first cannabis use. Education and employment one year before assessment may themselves reflect a developing illness, so adjusting for them may remove part of an effect or add bias.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls less often smoked 10 or more cigarettes a day (12.8% vs 32.9%) or had used stimulants (12.0% vs 21.8%), hallucinogens (9.0% vs 14.5%), ketamine (2.8% vs 6.1%) or legal highs (2.4% vs 4.3%) (Table 1); all were adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Case status: first presentation with an ICD-10 psychotic disorder (F20-F33), with a research diagnosis from the Operational Criteria Checklist (OPCRIT) for all cases interviewed. Ecological outcome: incidence rates of psychotic disorder adjusted for age, gender and ethnic minority status, from the EU-GEI incidence study (Jongsma et al., 2018).
outcomes.validity_norms: OPCRIT gives harmonized research diagnoses across sites; whether interviewers knew case status is not reported; cases were approached through their clinical teams.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychotic disorder = being a case; the attributable fractions and the incidence correlation treat first-episode psychosis in each catchment population as the outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six cannabis measures (crude and fully adjusted), a six-category combined measure of frequency and potency, interaction tests, 22 site-specific odds ratios and attributable fractions, and three site-level correlations, all judged at p < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; recruitment materials for cases and controls did not mention cannabis (Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Fully adjusted odds ratios (Table 2): lifetime use 1.3 (1.1 to 1.6); current use 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); first use at 15 or younger 1.6 (1.1 to 2.1); use more than once a week 1.4 (1.0 to 2.0) and daily use 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1), both against never or occasional use; spending €20 or more a week 2.5 (1.6 to 3.8); low-potency cannabis 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) and high-potency cannabis 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), both against never use. The corresponding age, gender and ethnicity adjusted values are 2.45, 2.7, 3.9, 2.5, 6.2, 5.6, 2.0 and 3.2. Combined measure (Figure 1, fully adjusted, against never use): occasional low-potency 0.84, occasional high-potency 0.96, more than weekly 1.36 and 1.57, daily low-potency 2.19 (1.4 to 3.6), daily high-potency 4.78 (2.5 to 6.3). Site-specific daily-use odds ratios 1.1 to 7.1 and high-potency odds ratios 0.6 to 3.6, with no significant variation by site (p = 0.25 and 0.45) (Table 3). Attributable fractions assuming causality: high-potency use 12.2% (3.0 to 16.1) and daily use 20.4% (17.6 to 22.0) in the whole sample (Table 3). Site-level correlations with adjusted incidence: r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109) for daily use and r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286) for high-potency use (Results, 15th and 16th paragraphs).
analysis.covariates: Age, gender and ethnicity (first stage, labelled crude); education, employment status, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs and hallucinogens added in the full models (Table 2 footnote). Cluster-robust estimation by site; inverse-probability weights for controls (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned in the main text.
analysis.selective_reporting: The combined frequency-and-potency measure was built after the two measures with the highest odds ratios were identified (Results, 9th paragraph). The appendix (a PDF, not read) holds the site and catchment details, the questionnaire, the construction of the potency measure, the weighting, the confounder selection, the comparison of refusers, site-level recruitment and the probabilistic bias analysis; the statement that selection bias is unlikely, the potency classification and the timing of exposure rest on it. The response of controls is not reported, no attributable fraction is given for daily high-potency use, and incidence values for six of the ten correlated sites appear only in Figure 3.
analysis.power: Not reported. The authors say the absence of interaction with site may reflect insufficient power (Discussion, 1st paragraph); site samples are small (Paris 54 cases and 100 controls; Bologna 65 controls), and each ecological correlation rests on 10 site-level points.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Daily use (against never or occasional use) and use of high-potency types (against never use) were reported more often by people with first-episode psychosis than by population controls: fully adjusted odds ratios 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) and 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), and 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) for daily high-potency use; ever use 1.3 (1.1 to 1.6); occasional use of either potency was not associated (0.84 and 0.96). Full adjustment roughly halved every estimate. Site-specific odds ratios varied widely, with wide intervals and no significant interaction with site. Across 10 sites, the prevalence of daily and of high-potency use among controls correlated with adjusted incidence (printed r 0.8 and 0.7).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's interpretation says differences in daily and high-potency use “contributed to the striking variation” in incidence, the Research-in-context box calls the study “the first direct evidence that cannabis use has an effect on variation in the incidence”, and the conclusion says the findings show how cannabis use affects incidence (Summary › Interpretation; Research in context; Discussion, 12th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the causal statements about incidence rest on an ecological correlation of 10 site-level points (Puy de Dôme excluded), using two exposure measures that are themselves strongly correlated across sites (see reporting issues); (2) the attributable fractions are labelled as assuming causality, but the abstract's figures for cases that could be prevented (12.2% overall, 30.3% in London, 50.3% in Amsterdam) also assume unconfounded odds ratios and no switch to other cannabis; (3) the abstract compares daily use with people who never used cannabis, whereas the reference group in Table 2 is never or occasional use; (4) the discussion calls high-potency use a strong predictor in Paris, where the odds ratio was 2.1 (0.8 to 3.6); (5) the bias analysis presented as showing selection bias is unlikely used an odds ratio (5.7) that matches neither the crude nor the adjusted daily-use estimate; (6) not mentioning cannabis in recruitment materials is said to avoid selection and recall bias altogether (Discussion, 11th paragraph), which it cannot; (7) residual confounding, reverse causation and the genetic evidence are not discussed as limitations.

timeline.event: Boydell et al. (Psychological Medicine): trends in cannabis use before first presentation with schizophrenia in south-east London, 1965 to 1999; described in this paper's Research-in-context box as speculating that rising incidence of schizophrenia might relate to rising cannabis use.
Di Forti et al. (British Journal of Psychiatry): the team's first south London report that high-potency cannabis carried the highest risk (ref 15).

Di Forti et al. (Lancet Psychiatry): south London case-control study, attributable fraction of 24% for high-potency cannabis assuming causality; the finding this study set out to replicate (ref 28; card sc_di_forti_2015). Same team and same London catchment, so the two are not independent.
Marconi et al. meta-analysis, cited as showing a dose-response association with the highest odds in the heaviest use (Introduction, 1st paragraph; card sc_marconi_2016).

Ksir and Hart critical overview, cited with Hill (2015) and Boydell et al. (2006) for the view that it is unclear whether patterns of cannabis use influence population rates of psychotic disorder (Introduction, 1st paragraph).
Gage, Hickman and Zammit review, cited with Mustonen et al. (2018) as epidemiological evidence supporting a causal link (Introduction, 1st paragraph).

Jongsma et al. (JAMA Psychiatry): EU-GEI incidence study reporting an eight-fold variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across the study sites; source of the incidence rates correlated here.

Linked comment by Gage, 'Cannabis and psychosis: triangulating the evidence' (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30086-0), read on the publisher site: welcomes the design but notes uncertainty in the potency variable, small site samples (15 to 201 cases per site), no association with less-than-weekly use whatever the potency, genetic evidence consistent with shared aetiology, prodromal symptoms before first use not ruled out, and Mendelian-randomization evidence suggesting a bidirectional relation.

Letter by Sommer and van den Brink (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30130-0): the attributable fractions treat the odds ratios as wholly causal despite likely residual confounding by genetic vulnerability; cite a two-sample bidirectional Mendelian randomization study (Pasman et al., 2018) pointing from schizophrenia to cannabis use, and the lower odds ratio in Gouda and Voorhout than in Amsterdam (1.5 vs 3.6) as signs of overestimation.

Letter by Gillespie, Pasman, Treur, Derks, Verweij and Vink (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30174-9; corrected for an author's name, correction doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30225-1): genetic correlation of 0.25 between lifetime cannabis use and schizophrenia, bidirectional Mendelian randomization supporting an effect of schizophrenia liability on cannabis use with little evidence for the reverse (with a weaker instrument and no frequency or potency data), a Swedish co-relative study (Giordano et al., 2015) attributing much of the association to familial confounding, and no rise in schizophrenia in Australia as cannabis use rose (Degenhardt et al., 2003).

Letter by Linnman (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30175-0): proposes nitrogen oxides in tobacco and cannabis smoke and in urban air as a common alternative explanation, citing the tobacco odds ratio in this study's appendix and his own unpublished crude ecological correlation across the EU-GEI regions.
Letter by Clark (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30178-6): cannabis samples were not tested for cannabinoids or contaminants, and cases used more other drugs.

Authors' reply by Di Forti, Morgan, Selten, Lynskey and Murray (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30176-2): attributable fractions for component causes can sum to more than 100%; population controls are the correct comparison; the tobacco effect was concentrated in the Spanish and Italian sites; other Mendelian randomization studies (Vaucher et al., 2018) disagree with Pasman et al., whose phenotype was ever use only; contaminants were unlikely to be the same across sites and other drugs were adjusted for.

replication.where_it_stands: The largest case-control study of cannabis frequency and potency in first-episode psychosis. Its individual-level association replicates the same team's south London finding (overlapping investigators and catchment, so not independent replication); the incidence correlation is ecological and has no replication in the sources read. The published critiques of 2019 challenge the causal assumption behind the attributable fractions with genetic-correlation, Mendelian-randomization and co-relative evidence; the authors' reply disputes the relevance of ever-use genetic phenotypes. The paper itself discusses no genetic or quasi-experimental test. Claims should give the adjusted odds ratios with their reference groups, and the attributable fractions only as figures that assume causality.

funding.affiliations_note: Led from King's College London (Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience), with authors from centres in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy, Brazil and Hong Kong. The first and last authors (Di Forti, Murray) also led the south London studies whose finding this study replicates; Tom P Freeman, who wrote the Lancet Psychiatry comment on the 2015 study, is a co-author. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that measures frequency and biologically verified potency (THC and CBD) of cannabis use from adolescence, records psychotic-like symptoms before first use, and has family-history and polygenic data, ideally with sibling or co-twin comparisons; and, for the population claim, repeated measurement within sites showing whether changes in daily and high-potency use are followed by changes in incidence.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drug use, but not for family history or genetic liability, childhood adversity or premorbid functioning; full adjustment roughly halved every odds ratio, which shows how sensitive the estimates are to measured confounders and makes residual confounding plausible. Use during a prodrome (reverse causation) is not addressed, and education and employment may be affected by the illness itself.

Retrospective self-report of a lifetime pattern after a first psychotic episode, without biological verification; potency assigned from national mean THC for the type named, dichotomized at 10%, without CBD; the timing of the pattern relative to onset is not stated in the main text. Recruitment materials did not mention cannabis, which limits but does not remove differential recall.

Incident cases from defined catchments, but 23% refused, and refusers differed by age, sex and ethnicity; control response is not reported; quota sampling with advertising top-ups and weights. The bias analysis that the authors cite is not applied to the main estimate (see reporting issues).
No intervention between exposure and outcome is relevant to this comparison.

Complete-case analysis; six of 17 sites excluded (five for at least 10% missing data), so 229 of 1130 cases and 262 of 1499 controls were not analysed; no comparison of included and excluded participants or imputation is reported in the main text.
First-episode psychosis with ICD-10 diagnoses harmonized by OPCRIT; the incidence rates come from a separate standardized study.
Six exposure measures, a combined measure built after seeing which measures had the largest odds ratios, many site-level estimates and attributable fractions, and no registered analysis plan.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large incident-case study with harmonized diagnoses and a population-based control strategy, so the reported associations are well documented as associations; but they remain open to residual confounding and reverse causation, which no part of the study addresses. The attributable fractions add the assumption that the adjusted odds ratios are causal, and the incidence analysis adds an ecological inference from 10 sites. The paper may be cited for the adjusted odds ratios with their reference groups, for the absence of an association with occasional use, and for the site differences in the prevalence of daily and high-potency use; it should not be cited for the share of cases caused by cannabis, or for cannabis use explaining variation in incidence.

key_findings.finding: Of 1519 people with first-episode psychosis approached between 1 May 2010 and 1 April 2015, 356 (23%) refused, 19 could not consent because of language and 14 were outside the age range; 1130 took part. Refusers were older, more often women and more often of white European origin; participants were younger than the full incidence sample (mean 31.2 vs 34.5 years). 1499 controls were recruited at 16 of the 17 sites.

After excluding Maison Blanche (no controls) and five sites with at least 10% missing data on cannabis or main confounders (Verona, Santiago, Oviedo, Valencia, Cuenca), 901 cases and 1237 controls in 11 sites were analysed as complete cases.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 229 of 1130 cases (20%) and 262 of 1499 controls (17%) were not analysed.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime cannabis use was reported by 574 of 1237 controls (46.4%) and 585 of 901 cases (64.9%); smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day by 12.8% and 32.9%; ever use of stimulants by 12.0% and 21.8%, hallucinogens 9.0% and 14.5%, ketamine 2.8% and 6.1%, legal highs 2.4% and 4.3%. Cases were younger, more often men and from ethnic minorities, less educated and more often unemployed.

Lifetime use: odds ratio 2.45 (2.0 to 2.9) adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity, and 1.3 (1.1 to 1.6) fully adjusted (p = 0.0225). Current use: 2.7 (2.1 to 3.5) and 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) (p = 0.36). First use at 15 or younger: 3.9 (3.0 to 4.9) and 1.6 (1.1 to 2.1) (p = 0.0122).
key_findings.note: Table 2 labels the first-stage estimates crude, but they are adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity; the full models add education, employment, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs and hallucinogens (Table 2 footnote).

key_findings.finding: Lifetime frequency (most consistent pattern), against never or occasional use: more than once a week 2.5 (1.9 to 3.5), fully adjusted 1.4 (1.0 to 2.0), p = 0.066; daily use 6.2 (4.8 to 8.2), fully adjusted 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1), p < 0.0001. Daily use was reported by 84 of 1237 controls (6.8%) and 266 of 901 cases (29.5%).
key_findings.note: The reference group for frequency is never or occasional use (1061 controls, 528 cases), not never use as the abstract states; by the editors' arithmetic it includes about 411 controls and 225 cases who had used cannabis occasionally.

key_findings.finding: The daily-use odds ratio changed little when age at first use (3.1, 2.1 to 5.2), money spent (2.9, 1.9 to 4.4) or type of cannabis (2.6, 2.0 to 3.9) were added. Spending €20 or more a week (2.5, 1.6 to 3.8) fell to 1.3 (1.0 to 2.1) after adjustment for daily use and type; no interaction between daily use and spending (p = 0.67).

Potency, against never use: low-potency cannabis (THC below 10%) 2.0 (1.6 to 2.5), fully adjusted 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5), p = 0.38; high-potency cannabis (THC 10% or more) 3.2 (2.6 to 4.0), fully adjusted 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), p = 0.0032, and 1.5 (1.1 to 2.6) after also adjusting for daily use. Starting high-potency use by age 15: 2.3 (1.4 to 3.1), no interaction (p = 0.63). High-potency use was reported by 240 controls (19.4%) and 334 cases (37.1%).
key_findings.note: The main text speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency, not of the type mainly used: in Table 2 every person who had used is in one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, potency missing for 3; 251 + 334 = 585 cases; editors' arithmetic), and how people who used both types were classed is described only in the appendix (not read).

key_findings.finding: Combined frequency and potency, fully adjusted odds ratios against never use: occasional use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (THC 10% or more); use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57; daily use 2.19 (1.4 to 3.6) and 4.78 (2.5 to 6.3). The corresponding age, gender and ethnicity adjusted values are 0.93, 1.11, 1.71, 2.12, 3.08 and 5.81. No interaction between frequency and type (p = 0.25).
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph; Figure 1 (value labels, read on screen)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 labels the occasional categories 'rare use'. Intervals are printed in the text only for the two daily categories; the others are shown only as error bars.

key_findings.finding: Neither the daily-use nor the high-potency odds ratio varied significantly by site (p = 0.25 and 0.45). Fully adjusted daily-use odds ratios ranged from 7.1 (3.4 to 11.8) in Amsterdam to 1.1 (0.4 to 12.2) in Puy de Dôme, and high-potency odds ratios from 3.6 (1.5 to 7.7) in Amsterdam to 0.6 (0.1 to 2.5) in Palermo; London 3.6 (1.4 to 4.4) and 2.4 (1.4 to 4.0); Paris 2.8 (1.7 to 12.3) and 2.1 (0.8 to 3.6).

In the three sites with the most high-potency use, the fully adjusted odds ratio for daily high-potency use against never use was 5.16 in London (201 cases, 230 controls), 9.43 in Amsterdam (96 cases, 101 controls) and 4.28 in Paris (54 cases, 100 controls).
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph; Figure 2 (value labels and legend, read on screen)
key_findings.note: Intervals are not printed; read approximately from the error bars, they run from about 3.0 to 12 (London), 6 to 20 (Amsterdam) and 2.1 to 15 (Paris).

key_findings.finding: Attributable fractions assuming causality: whole sample, high-potency use 12.2% (3.0 to 16.1) and daily use 20.4% (17.6 to 22.0); London 30.3% (15.2 to 40.0) and 21.0% (11.1 to 31.2); Amsterdam 50.3% (27.4 to 66.0) and 43.8% (34.0 to 69.1); lowest for high-potency use 1.9% (Bologna and Ribeirão Preto) and for daily use 1.2% (Puy de Dôme); not calculated for high-potency use in Palermo, where there was no main effect.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results, 12th and 13th paragraphs; Summary › Findings
key_findings.note: Editors' check: the printed fractions match the case-based formula (prevalence of exposure in cases × [1 − 1/odds ratio]) within about one percentage point, using the case prevalences in Table 3 (for example Amsterdam, 69.6% × 2.6/3.6 = 50.3%).

key_findings.finding: Across sites, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder correlated with the prevalence of daily use in controls (r = 0.8, p = 0.0109) and of high-potency use (r = 0.7, p = 0.0286). London (daily use in 26 of 223 controls, 11.7%; high-potency 58 of 223) had 45.7 cases per 100,000 person-years, Amsterdam (13 of 100 daily; 54 of 100 high-potency) 37.9, Paris (21 of 100 high-potency) 46.1 and Bologna (3 of 65 daily, 4.6%) 21.0.
key_findings.note: Figure 3 plots 10 sites (Puy de Dôme excluded for missing ethnicity data). The printed p-values correspond to r of about 0.76 and 0.69 with 10 sites (editors' calculation); with 11 sites, p = 0.0109 would correspond to r of about 0.73.

key_findings.finding: The probabilistic sensitivity analysis for selection bias gave a corrected odds ratio for daily use of 5.7 (3.5 to 9.4), against an original 5.7 (4.4 to 7.5); the authors conclude selection bias is unlikely to explain the findings.
key_findings.note: Neither value matches the daily-use odds ratios in Table 2 (6.2 adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity; 3.2 fully adjusted); the details are in the appendix, not read.

key_findings.finding: Assuming causality, the authors estimate that without high-potency cannabis the adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder would fall from 37.9 to 18.8 cases per 100,000 person-years in Amsterdam and from 45.7 to 31.9 in London.

Limitations stated by the authors: no biological validation of self-report; potency based on official estimates of mean THC by type, without CBD (reliable data only for England and the Netherlands); a 10% cut-off that they call conservative and that may underestimate the effect of potency in the UK and the Netherlands; weights for oversampling, most sites having oversampled people aged 16 to 24.

The authors give THC contents of up to 67% for Nederhasj and 22% for Nederwiet in the Netherlands, and state that skunk-like cannabis with an average THC of 14% made up 94% of the London street market, while herbal types below 10% THC were still common in Italy, France and Spain.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures, from refs 17, 18 and 29 (EMCDDA 2016; Spanish national report; Potter et al., 2018), not measured in this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion compare daily use with people who never used cannabis, but the reference category for lifetime frequency in Table 2 is never or occasional use (1061 controls, 528 cases), which includes about 411 controls and 225 cases who had used cannabis occasionally (editors' arithmetic from Table 2).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) is daily use against never-or-occasional use; claims must state that reference group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results describe the incidence correlations as across 11 sites, but Figure 3 excludes Puy de Dôme, leaving 10; the printed p-values (0.0109 and 0.0286) fit r of about 0.76 and 0.69 with 10 sites, which the paper rounds to 0.8 and 0.7 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Results, 15th and 16th paragraphs; Figure 3 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Each ecological correlation rests on 10 points; the rounded r values overstate the daily-use correlation.

reporting_issues.issue: The prevalences of daily use and of high-potency use in controls are said to be only modestly correlated across sites (r = 0.2, p = 0.0413). A correlation of 0.2 gives p of about 0.56 to 0.58 with 10 or 11 sites (p = 0.04 would need about 100 observations), and the site prevalences in Table 3 give r of about 0.71 for the 10 plotted sites (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two site-level exposures are strongly collinear, so the two incidence correlations are not separate pieces of evidence, and the stated reason for reporting both does not hold.

reporting_issues.issue: The selection-bias analysis reports an original daily-use odds ratio of 5.7 (4.4 to 7.5), which matches neither the age, gender and ethnicity adjusted (6.2, 4.8 to 8.2) nor the fully adjusted (3.2, 2.2 to 4.1) estimates in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysis cited to show that selection bias is unlikely was not applied to the estimate the conclusions rest on.

reporting_issues.issue: The whole-sample attributable fraction for high-potency use is given as 12.2% (3.0 to 16.1) in the Summary and Table 3 but as 12.2% (3.0 to 6.1) in the Results.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 12th paragraph; Table 3; Summary › Findings

reporting_issues.issue: The same quantities differ between places: high-potency use in 19.4% of controls and 37.1% of cases in Table 2, but 19.1% and 35.1% in Table 3; daily use in Bologna controls 4.1% in Table 3 but 3 of 65 (4.6%) in the text; London controls 223 in the text but 230 in the Figure 2 legend, Amsterdam 100 and 101.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; Table 3; Results, 15th paragraph; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Small differences, but they show that the site-level inputs to the attributable fractions and correlations cannot be reconciled exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 3 does not match the text and Table 3 at some sites (approximate reading of the image): Paris's adjusted incidence is plotted at about 41 to 42 per 100,000 person-years, below London, while the text gives 46.1, above London's 45.7; daily-use prevalence in controls is plotted at about 6% for Barcelona and 10% for Paris against 8.3% and 11.6% in Table 3.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figure 3; Results, 16th paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The data behind the correlations are uncertain; the incidence values should be taken from the EU-GEI incidence paper rather than from this one.

reporting_issues.issue: The χ² p-value for current cannabis use (132 of 1237 controls, 10.7%, vs 198 of 901 cases, 22.0%) is printed as 0.00349; these proportions give p < 0.0001 (z about 7.1, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misprint; no effect on the odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol is reported as 5.2 drinks a day (SD 0.4) among controls and 4.8 (SD 0.4) among cases with p = 0.45, but with SDs of 0.4 in groups of this size the difference would give t of about 23; the p-value fits only if 0.4 is a standard error. Alcohol is also named among the confounders in the Methods but is absent from the Table 2 adjustment footnote.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 5th paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 footnote
reporting_issues.consequence: The alcohol figures and the adjustment set are reported inconsistently; claims should list the adjustment set from the Table 2 footnote.

reporting_issues.issue: Several fully adjusted intervals are not centred on their point estimates on the log scale, as Wald intervals from logistic regression would be: daily use 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1), geometric centre about 3.0; daily high-potency use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3), centre about 4.0; London daily use 3.6 (1.4 to 4.4), centre about 2.5; Madrid daily use 2.5 (2.1 to 7.3), centre about 3.9 (editors' calculation). The method for the intervals is not described.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; Table 3; Results, 9th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the intervals or some point estimates are misprinted, or a different method was used; the precision of the headline estimates cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: At sites where the odds-ratio interval includes 1, the attributable-fraction interval nevertheless excludes 0: Paris high-potency use 2.1 (0.8 to 3.6) with 18.9% (14.6 to 36.0), marked significant; Gouda and Voorhout 1.5 (0.8 to 3.1) with 12.2% (8.7 to 25.3), marked significant; Cambridge daily use 2.2 (0.8 to 6.5) with 10.4% (4.7 to 21.0), marked significant. The problem is general: every site-level fraction in Table 3 has an interval above zero, including 13 site estimates whose odds-ratio interval includes 1 (8 for high-potency use, 5 for daily use; editors' count), for example Madrid high-potency use 2.0 (0.7 to 5.7) with 17.2% (0.9 to 25.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: The attributable-fraction intervals understate uncertainty; site-level fractions marked significant should not be cited as such.

reporting_issues.issue: Text errors in the Discussion: daily use of high-potency cannabis is said to be associated with a doubling of the odds in the whole sample, but that odds ratio is 4.8 and the doubling (2.2) belongs to daily low-potency use (2nd paragraph); the attributable fraction for daily use is said to range from 44% in Amsterdam to 6% in Palermo, whereas the lowest in Table 3 is 1.2% in Puy de Dôme, and the London figure is called similar to one previously reported, citing reference 3, a review of cannabis legalization, rather than the team's 2015 study (6th paragraph).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should take figures from the tables, not from the Discussion text.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion (1st paragraph) says that starting by 15 raised the odds modestly but not independently of frequency of use or of potency, but no estimate for first use at 15 or younger adjusted for daily use or potency is printed; only the reverse adjustment (daily use 3.1, 2.1 to 5.2, after adding age at first use) and starting high-potency use by 15 (2.3, 1.4 to 3.1) are given.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that early first use adds nothing beyond frequency or potency is not shown by a printed estimate; claims should say that this was not shown, not that it was tested and found absent.
